title: Pricing, Dues, and Branch Pricing
how_it_works_companion: How It Works chapter 7, section HOW PRICING AND DUES WORK

sections.business_context:
A level has five money figures: an application fee, a joining fee, monthly dues, annual dues, and the
markup applied when the club fuels a car. Together they are what a member is quoted when they join
and what they pay when they renew.
This guide covers how those figures are held, how the same level can cost different amounts in
different cities, and how a price increase is entered so that it reaches members at the right moment
and no sooner.
The rule that governs the whole subject: a price change takes effect at renewal only. It never reaches
a member mid-period, never prorates, and never alters a payment schedule that is already running.
That is a commercial promise as much as a technical rule, and everything here exists to keep it.
Pairs with How It Works chapter 7, section HOW PRICING AND DUES WORK.

THE THREE-PART KEY

Column                          What it scopes

membership_level_id             Which level this price is for.

branch_id                       Which branch. Empty means the standard price at every branch.

effective_from                  From when. A renewal reads the row effective on its own date.



The three together are unique. One level may therefore hold a standard price and a New York price,
each with its own history of dated rows, and none of them ever overwrites another.
sections.implementation_workflow:
1) Setting a Standard Price
    1. Create the row with the level, no branch, an effective date, and all five figures.
    2. A row with no branch is the standard price for that level everywhere. It is the row that must
       exist before any branch-specific row is permitted.
    3. All five figures are required and none may be negative. A fee of zero is legitimate and is not
       the same as an absent figure.
    4. The effective date may be today or in the future, never in the past. Backdating a price would
       change what somebody was already quoted.

2) Setting a Branch Price
    1. Create a second row for the same level with a branch and its own effective date.
    2. A branch row overrides the standard for that market only. Every other branch continues on the
       standard row.
    3. The branch row carries all five figures, not only the ones that differ. A branch that does not
       vary the fuel markup repeats it.
    4. A branch price with no availability row for that branch is a data error. The price could never be
       quoted, because the level cannot be sold there.
    5. A level with no branch row for a city simply uses the standard figure. Absence means
       standard, not unavailable.
    6. A member who relocates picks up their new branch’s price at their next renewal, never mid-
       period, so they end up paying what everyone else at that location pays.
    7. Refuse a branch row where no standard row exists for the level, or the club ends up with a
       level priced in one city and nowhere else.

3) Entering an Increase
    1. An increase is a new row with a later effective date, not an edit to an existing one. The
       previous row stays and remains the answer for any date before the change.
    2. The entry screen offers a percentage or a direct amount. The percentage is an entry aid: it
       calculates the figures and shows them for review, and only the resulting amounts are stored.
    3. Select the level, and either every branch or one branch. An increase in one market leaves
       every other market alone.


    4. Set the effective date. A future date is the ordinary case: entered in November, effective the
       first of January.
    5. Nothing happens to any existing member at the moment the row is saved. New sales quote
       the new figure from the effective date; existing members meet it at their own renewal.

4) Reading a Price
    1. At joining, read the price for the level at the enrolling branch, effective on the enrollment date.
    2. At renewal, read the price for the level at the member’s current home branch, effective on the
       renewal date.
    3. Prefer a branch row over the standard row. Where no branch row is effective on that date, the
       standard row is the answer.
    4. Read at no other time. A running package prices its dues from its own payment schedule,
       which was built at activation or at the last renewal.
    5. A member who transferred branches during the period meets their new branch’s price at their
       next renewal, which is when the transfer finally reaches their bill.

5) Negotiated Prices and Increases
    1. Where a member holds a pricing customization still in force after the effective date, they are
       not moved to the new catalog figure.
    2. What happens at renewal is decided by the scope on the customization. A first Year (Period)
       or Current Year (Period) rate simply ends, and the member renews at the standard figure with
       nothing to review.
    3. An every package rate continues through the increase. The renewal leaves the negotiated
       figure in place and raises a task naming the member, what they pay, and what the new catalog
       price is, so a permanent discount surviving a price rise is a decision somebody makes rather
       than one nobody notices.
    4. A person decides, because only a person knows whether the discount was agreed as a fixed
       amount or as a fixed gap below the standard price.
    5. Customizations scoped to a first or current package expire on their own and need no attention.
sections.rules_and_constraints:
1. A price change takes effect at renewal only and never mid-period.
    2. The key is level, branch, and effective date together, and it is unique.
    3. A row with no branch is the standard price at every branch.
    4. A branch row requires a standard row for the same level to exist.
    5. Every row carries all five figures; a branch row repeats what it does not vary.
    6. Figures may be zero and may not be negative.
    7. An effective date may be today or future, never past.
    8. An increase is a new row, never an edit.
    9. A percentage is an entry aid; only amounts are stored.
    10. Pricing is read at joining and at renewal and at no other time.
    11. A branch row is preferred over the standard row for the same date.

    12. A branch price with no availability at that branch is a data error.
    13. A member with an in-force negotiated price is never moved automatically; where its scope is
        Every Year (Period), a task is raised.
    14. A member who relocates picks up their new branch’s price at their next renewal, never mid-
        period.
sections.integration_and_edge_cases:
1. An increase entered in November for January. The ordinary case. December renewals take
       the old figure and January renewals take the new one, with nobody having to act on the day.
    2. A member renewing on the effective date itself. The new row is effective on that date, so
       they take the new price. Effective from means from and including.
    3. A level with a New York price and no standard price. Refused. Every other branch would
       have nothing to quote.
    4. A branch price for a branch where the level is not sold. Nothing breaks and the price can
       never be used. Flag it rather than leaving it to be found.
    5. A member who moved from Houston to New York mid-period. They pay Houston prices
       until their renewal, then New York prices. The transfer reaches correspondence immediately
       and the bill later, deliberately.
    6. A price reduced rather than raised. Same mechanism entirely. The word increase is habit;
       the structure does not care about direction.
    7. A negotiated price below the old catalog figure when the catalog rises. The task exists
       precisely because the club has to decide whether the member keeps the amount or keeps the
       discount.
    8. Two rows for one level, branch, and date. Impossible; the key prevents it. Correcting a row
       entered in error means superseding it with another effective date, or deleting it before it has
       been used.

sections.developer_notes:
1. Renewal only. This is the whole guide. Any code path that reprices a running package has
       broken the dues doctrine, and the failure will show up as a member being billed something
       they never agreed to.
    2. Resolution has two steps. Filter to rows effective on or before the date, then prefer a branch
       row over the standard one. Doing it in one query with a coalesce is possible and much harder
       to read.
    3. From means from and including. A renewal on the effective date takes the new price. State
       it in the query rather than leaving it to whoever writes the comparison.
    4. Never edit a price row. Supersede it. Editing rewrites what somebody was quoted, and the
       shadow will show a change nobody can explain.
    5. The percentage is not stored. Only the resulting amounts. Storing a percentage invites
       somebody to recompute later against a different base.
    6. Zero is a price. A joining fee of zero is a real commercial decision. Do not treat it as missing.
    7. Availability and pricing are checked together at enrollment. A level needs both to be
       sellable, and the two failures deserve different messages.
sections.testing_checklist:
Setting Prices
    ☐ A branch row without a standard row for the same level is refused.
    ☐ A second row for the same level, branch, and effective date is refused.
    ☐ A price row with a past effective date is refused.
    ☐ A negative figure is refused; a zero figure is accepted.
    ☐ A branch price for a branch with no availability raises a warning.

Resolution
    ☐ A branch with no branch row resolves to the standard price.
    ☐ A branch with a branch row resolves to the branch price.
    ☐ A renewal on the effective date itself takes the new price.
    ☐ A renewal before the effective date takes the previous price.
    ☐ A future-dated question returns the price that will apply then.

Increases
    ☐ An increase creates a new row and leaves the previous one intact.
    ☐ Saving an increase lists the affected members before committing.
    ☐ No existing member’s payment schedule changes when the row is saved.
    ☐ A member renewing after the effective date takes the new figure.
    ☐ An increase applied to one branch leaves other branches unchanged.
    ☐ The percentage entry aid stores amounts only.

Negotiated Prices
    ☐ A member with an in-force pricing customization keeps their figure at renewal.
    ☐ A review task is raised naming the member and both figures.
    ☐ A first-package pricing customization expires without a task.
